ui.title: Theories
ui.intro: Short explanations of how training works: what each idea means, how to use it and what to avoid. Every theory has a short version and a detailed one.
ui.disclaimer: These theories are general education, not medical advice. If you have pain, an injury or a health condition, ask a doctor or physiotherapist before you change your training.

1.title: How Training Changes the Body
1.short: Training is a controlled challenge that pushes your nervous system, muscles, heart and other tissues to get better at the tasks you repeat. Progress comes from pairing that challenge with enough recovery and raising the demand gradually, not from making every workout exhausting.

2.title: Components of Physical Fitness
2.short: Physical fitness is made of several partly independent abilities: strength, power, muscular endurance, aerobic endurance, mobility, balance and coordination. Knowing them helps you pick exercises that match your goal, because different workouts train different things.

3.title: Training Goals: General Fitness, Strength, Conditioning
3.short: General fitness, strength and conditioning are different priorities, and each one shapes exercise choice, effort, rest and progression. You can train several qualities together, but one primary goal makes a program easier to organize and to judge.

4.title: Fitness Levels: Beginner, Intermediate, Advanced
4.short: Your training level describes your experience and skill with the exercises and workloads you actually do, not how athletic you look. Beginners usually progress with simple practice and modest volume, while experienced trainees often need more deliberate planning.

5.title: Readiness Check: When to Consult a Professional First
5.short: A readiness check spots health concerns or symptoms that may need professional advice before you exercise harder. It helps you make safer training decisions, but it is not a medical diagnosis and it does not automatically ban you from activity.

6.title: Physical Activity Guidelines
6.short: Physical activity guidelines set the minimum weekly activity linked to important health benefits. For most adults, a useful target is regular moderate or vigorous aerobic activity plus strength training for the major muscle groups on at least two days a week.

7.title: Setting Realistic Training Goals
7.short: A useful training goal is specific, measurable, realistic and tied to a time frame. Pair the result you want with weekly actions you control, so you can see progress even when results come slowly.

8.title: Consistency and Training Habits
8.short: Consistency means training often enough, for long enough, that improvements add up, including in imperfect weeks. Short workouts you can repeat and a predictable routine usually beat an ambitious plan you drop after a few sessions.

9.title: Major Muscle Groups
9.short: Your major muscle groups work together to move and stabilize your body, so training them takes more than isolating single muscles. Knowing what each group does helps you build balanced sessions and see why one movement can work several areas at once.

10.title: How Muscles Work: Concentric, Eccentric, Isometric
10.short: Muscles produce or resist force while shortening, lengthening or holding a position. These concentric, eccentric and isometric actions often happen within the same exercise, and they help explain what it means to control a weight.

11.title: Muscle Fiber Types
11.short: Skeletal muscles contain fibers that differ in fatigue resistance and force production, usually described as type I and type II. Both types help you move, and training improves how they perform without turning you into a completely different “fiber type.”

12.title: Joints and Range of Motion
12.short: Joints move within ranges shaped by anatomy, muscle control, flexibility and comfort. Training through a useful range you can control usually builds ability that carries over better than forcing everyone into the same positions.

13.title: The Spine, Core and Bracing
13.short: Your spine supports you and lets you move, and the trunk muscles around it help control forces during exercise. Bracing is a coordinated tightening of the trunk that can improve stability, and it is different from holding one rigid posture in every activity.

14.title: Energy Systems in Exercise
14.short: Exercise draws on three overlapping energy systems: phosphagen, glycolytic and oxidative. All three work all the time, but how much each one matters changes with how hard and how long you move and how much you recover between efforts.

15.title: Heart Rate and Training Zones
15.short: Heart rate can help you estimate how hard aerobic exercise is, but training zones are approximations, not universal biological boundaries. Use your pulse together with breathing, the talk test, effort and your own health factors to pick an intensity you can keep up.

16.title: Breathing During Exercise
16.short: Breathing supports movement, helps manage pressure in your trunk and changes with how hard you work. For most beginners, a steady rhythm and breathing out during the harder part of each rep is a practical way to avoid holding your breath when you don’t need to.

17.title: Motor Learning: How Technique Is Built
17.short: Exercise technique is a skill you build through repeated, attentive practice and useful feedback. You learn exercises more efficiently when you start with easier versions, keep your reps consistent, and make things harder only once you have control.

18.title: Muscle Growth (Hypertrophy)
18.short: Muscle hypertrophy is an increase in muscle size that comes from repeated training and recovery. Mechanical loading is a major stimulus, and training volume, effort, enough nutrition and sleep affect how much you can adapt.

19.title: Sets, Reps and Rest Periods
19.short: A rep is one movement of an exercise, a set is a group of reps, and rest periods separate sets or exercises. Together they decide how much work fits into a session and how well you can keep up your strength, technique or endurance.

20.title: Rep Ranges and What They Train
20.short: Rep ranges guide what you emphasize, but they don’t split training into strict categories. Heavier, low-rep work matters most for maximal strength, muscle can grow across many ranges, and high reps can build local muscular endurance.

21.title: Training Volume
21.short: Training volume is how much work you do. In resistance training it is usually counted as hard sets per muscle group per week. Enough volume drives progress, but sets beyond what you can recover from may lower the quality of your training.

22.title: Intensity: Load and Percentage of 1RM
22.short: Intensity in resistance training often means how heavy a load is compared with your one-repetition maximum, or 1RM. Experienced lifters can use percentages to set their loads. Beginners can pick a weight more safely from controlled reps and effort, without a maximal test.

23.title: Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE)
23.short: Rating of Perceived Exertion (RPE) is your own rating of how hard exercise feels. If you record it next to what you completed, you can spot sessions that were easier or harder than expected and adjust future training a little at a time.

24.title: Reps in Reserve (RIR)
24.short: Reps in Reserve (RIR) is your estimate of how many more clean reps you could have done before the end of a set. It helps you pick loads that are hard but leave a couple of reps to spare, without testing your maximum or going to failure on every set.

25.title: Lifting Tempo
25.short: Lifting tempo is the speed and timing of each phase of a rep. A controlled tempo helps you practice technique and makes workouts easier to repeat. Very slow reps are not automatically better for strength or muscle growth.

26.title: Timed Sets and Holds
26.short: Timed sets and static holds measure effort in seconds instead of reps. They suit planks, wall sits, hangs and conditioning intervals, as long as your position or pace stays the same for the whole time.

27.title: Training Frequency
27.short: Training frequency is how often you exercise in a week, counted overall or for one muscle group. A good schedule gives you enough practice and work to progress and still leaves time for recovery and the rest of your life.

28.title: Exercise Order in a Session
28.short: Exercise order decides which exercises get you at your freshest. Put your priority exercises, technically hard movements and high-force lifts early, then fit simpler assistance, core or conditioning work where it serves the session goal.

29.title: Training to Failure
29.short: Training to failure means continuing a set until you can’t complete another rep to the standard you chose. It takes a lot of effort, but you don’t need it for strength or muscle growth, and it adds fatigue and technique risks.

30.title: Planning Session Length
30.short: Planning session length means estimating how long your warm-up, sets, rests, exercise changes and any conditioning really take. A realistic 20- to 45-minute workout that covers your main priorities often does more for you than a longer plan that never fits your day.

31.title: Fundamental Movement Patterns
31.short: Movement patterns group exercises by what the body does instead of by single muscles. Squat, hinge, lunge, push, pull, carry, core stabilization and locomotion give you a practical way to choose a balanced set of exercises.

32.title: The Squat Pattern
32.short: A squat lowers and raises your body by bending and straightening the hips, knees and ankles together. Learning a squat that feels comfortable for your body helps with lifting, sitting and many lower-body strength exercises.

33.title: The Hip Hinge Pattern
33.short: A hip hinge bends mainly at the hips while you keep your trunk controlled. It is the base of deadlifts, Romanian deadlifts and kettlebell movements, and it trains the glutes and hamstrings to produce force.

34.title: Lunges and Single-Leg Training
34.short: Lunges, split squats and step-ups put more load on one leg than the other and challenge your balance and hip control. They can build practical lower-body strength and show differences between your left and right sides.

35.title: Horizontal Pushing
35.short: Horizontal pushing moves your arms forward from your torso, as in push-ups, chest presses and bench presses. It mainly trains the chest, triceps and front of the shoulders, and it asks for trunk and shoulder control.

36.title: Vertical Pushing
36.short: Vertical pushing drives resistance overhead, as in a dumbbell shoulder press, an overhead barbell press or a pike push-up. It trains shoulder and arm strength and needs your shoulder blades, trunk and hips to work together.

37.title: Horizontal Pulling
37.short: Horizontal pulling draws your hands or elbows toward your torso, as in rows. Rows train the upper back, lats, rear shoulders and elbow flexors, and they balance out many pressing exercises.

38.title: Vertical Pulling
38.short: Vertical pulling brings your elbows down from an overhead position, as in pull-ups, chin-ups and lat pulldowns. It mainly works the lats and upper back, with a lot of help from the arms and trunk.

39.title: Core Training: Anti-Extension, Anti-Rotation, Anti-Lateral Flexion
39.short: Core strength includes resisting unwanted movement as well as bending the torso. Anti-extension, anti-rotation and anti-lateral-flexion exercises train your trunk to stay controlled while forces act on it.

40.title: Loaded Carries
40.short: Loaded carries mean walking while you hold a weight, such as dumbbells or kettlebells. A carry is simple but hard work: it trains grip strength, trunk stability, posture and walking pattern together.

41.title: Isolation Exercises
41.short: Isolation exercises focus on movement at one main joint, such as a biceps curl or leg extension. They let you give a muscle extra practice or training volume on top of what multi-joint movements already give it.

42.title: Balancing Push and Pull
42.short: Push and pull movements train different but overlapping parts of the upper body. Doing both builds well-rounded strength and keeps your program from filling up with pressing exercises.

43.title: Principles of Training
43.short: Good training follows a few connected principles: specificity, progressive overload, individualization, recovery, consistency and reversibility. They are a more reliable guide than copying an advanced athlete’s routine.

44.title: Progressive Overload
44.short: Progressive overload means slowly making an exercise harder as your body adapts. You need it to keep improving, and you can apply it through repetitions, resistance, movement control, range of motion or a harder exercise, as well as heavier weights.

45.title: Double Progression
45.short: Double progression is a simple way to move forward in strength training: you add repetitions within a chosen range, then add weight. It takes most of the guesswork out of picking a new load.

46.title: Full-Body, Upper/Lower and Split Programs
46.short: A training split is how you spread your exercises across the week. Full-body, upper/lower and muscle-group splits can all build strength and muscle when the total work, effort and recovery suit you.

47.title: Structuring a Training Week
47.short: A training week arranges hard sessions, easier activity and recovery so your plan fits your real life. A good schedule keeps you training often enough without piling up fatigue from hard workouts back to back.

48.title: Periodization Basics
48.short: Periodization means planning how your training stress changes over time. Linear, undulating and block approaches are ways to organize progress, but beginners can often improve with a much simpler program they stick to.

49.title: Deload Weeks
49.short: A deload is a short period of lighter training that lets fatigue drop while you keep practicing your movements. You can plan deloads ahead or use one when your normal workload stops feeling like something you recover from.

50.title: Choosing Exercises
50.short: Choose exercises that fit your goal, training level, equipment, space and any limitations you have. The best exercise is one you can do safely, repeat regularly and slowly make harder.

51.title: Progressions and Regressions
51.short: A progression makes an exercise harder, and a regression makes it easier. Both are normal coaching tools for matching an exercise to your strength, technique and recovery.

52.title: Supersets and Circuits
52.short: A superset pairs exercises with little rest between them, and a circuit rotates through several movements. Both can save time, but the fatigue and shorter recovery may lower the quality of heavy or very technical exercises.

53.title: Training Plateaus
53.short: A training plateau is a stretch of time when an ability stops improving even though you keep practicing. Plateaus are common, and the cause can be recovery, too little challenge, inconsistent measuring, or the slower progress that comes with experience.

54.title: Detraining and Returning After a Break
54.short: Detraining is the partial loss of fitness after you cut back or stop training. A careful return rebuilds your capacity step by step, without expecting your body to handle its old workload straight away.

55.title: Bodyweight Training
55.short: Bodyweight training uses your own body as resistance for strength and movement practice. Squats, push-ups, lunges, planks and pull-ups can take you a long way without buying a full set of weights.

56.title: Dumbbell Training
56.short: Dumbbells are versatile free weights for presses, rows, squats, hinges and single-leg exercises. Each arm moves on its own and you can change your grip, but you need to pay attention to balance, handling and storage.

57.title: Kettlebell Training
57.short: A kettlebell is a weight with a handle and its mass offset from the grip. You can use it for controlled strength exercises and for faster movements such as swings, but the more technical exercises take deliberate practice.

58.title: Resistance Band Training
58.short: Resistance bands give you portable resistance that usually gets stronger as the band stretches. You can use them for presses, rows, pulls and accessory work, as long as you anchor them safely and keep them in good condition.

59.title: Barbell Training
59.short: A barbell lets you load lifts such as squats, deadlifts, presses and rows a little heavier over time. It is good for building a high level of strength, but you need sound technique, a correct equipment setup and safety precautions.

60.title: Machines and Cable Training
60.short: Weight machines and cable stations give you adjustable resistance and can make exercise setup simpler. They are effective strength-training tools alongside free weights, not a lesser substitute.

61.title: Pull-Up Bar: Installation and Safety
61.short: A pull-up bar lets you do pull-ups, chin-ups and hanging exercises, but only if it is securely installed and rated for how you use it. How well it is mounted matters more than how many reps you can do.

62.title: Benches, Steps and Jump Ropes
62.short: Benches, steps and jump ropes add many exercises at home and in the gym. Each one works well only when its size, stability and clearance fit the movement and the person using it.

63.title: Choosing the Right Load
63.short: The right load is heavy enough to make you work and light enough that every rep stays controlled. As a beginner, you can choose weights by how well you move and how many reps you have left, without testing a maximal lift.

64.title: Training With Household Substitutes
64.short: Household objects can sometimes stand in for training equipment as light resistance or support. Use one only after you have checked its stability, how much load it holds, its grip and what you plan to do with it.

65.title: Usable Space and Exercise Clearance
65.short: Usable training space covers where you stand and also everywhere your body and equipment travel during each rep. Measuring it helps you avoid collisions and lets TrainUp pick exercises that really fit.

66.title: Ceiling Height and Overhead Exercises
66.short: Ceiling height decides whether overhead presses, pull-ups, jumps and rope skipping are practical. A movement can fit while you stand still and become unsafe once your arms, the load or your body move upward.

67.title: Training Surface and Footwear
67.short: Your floor and shoes affect stability, grip and how hard each landing feels. The best combination depends on whether the movement is mainly lifting, running, jumping or slow mobility work.

68.title: Noise and Impact When Training at Home
68.short: Home workouts can disturb neighbors and pound the floor, mostly through jumping and dropped weights. Lower-impact exercises still give you real conditioning with much less noise.

69.title: Training in a Gym: Etiquette and Safety
69.short: Training safely in a gym means good technique plus care for shared equipment and the people around you. Clear etiquette lowers the risk of injury and makes equipment easier for everyone to use when it is busy.

70.title: Training Outdoors: Weather and Terrain
70.short: Outdoors, the weather, ground, light and equipment all change from day to day. Adjusting how hard you go and where you go makes walks, runs and park workouts safer and easier to keep up.

71.title: Building an Aerobic Base
71.short: An aerobic base is your ability to keep up fairly comfortable activity for a long time. Building it makes everyday movement and harder conditioning sessions easier to handle.

72.title: Steady-State Cardio
72.short: Steady-state cardio keeps your effort fairly even for the whole session, through activities such as walking, jogging, cycling or cardio machines. It builds endurance without repeated all-out intervals.

73.title: Interval Training
73.short: Interval training alternates harder work with easier recovery. By setting how long and how hard each part is, you can improve your conditioning step by step, and no session has to be an all-out test.

74.title: HIIT and Tabata
74.short: High-intensity interval training (HIIT) alternates truly hard efforts with recovery, and Tabata is one specific format of 20 seconds of work and 10 seconds of rest. Neither term means just any fast workout.

75.title: Work-to-Rest Ratios
75.short: A work-to-rest ratio compares how long you work with how long you recover. Ratios such as 1:3, 1:1 and 2:1 decide how packed a workout feels, and their effect also depends on how hard the work interval is.

76.title: Low-Impact Conditioning
76.short: Low-impact conditioning raises your breathing and heart rate with fewer hard landings. It suits beginners, people who need to limit impact, and anyone training where noise is a problem.

77.title: Plyometrics and Jumping
77.short: Plyometrics train explosive movement through a fast stretch and shortening of the muscles, usually with hops, bounds and jumps. They need controlled landings, a gradual build-up and enough rest to keep every rep sharp.

78.title: Running Technique Basics
78.short: Running technique is about posture, stride timing and getting used to repeated impact a little at a time. As a beginner, you gain more from comfortable, repeatable running and a gradual build-up than from copying one “perfect” foot strike.

79.title: Jump Rope Skills
79.short: Jump rope is portable conditioning that takes rope timing and small, repeated hops. Get the rope length, wrist control and landing rhythm right before you try long or fast intervals.

80.title: Combining Strength and Cardio
80.short: Doing both resistance training and cardio builds muscular and cardiovascular fitness. For most recreational exercisers, a sensible weekly schedule lets you improve at both, so you do not have to choose one.

81.title: The Warm-Up
81.short: A warm-up gets your breathing, circulation, joints, muscles and coordination ready for the work ahead. A short general warm-up followed by a rehearsal of the exercise you are about to do usually helps more than a fixed set of stretches.

82.title: The Cool-Down
82.short: A cool-down eases your body from hard activity back toward rest with easy movement and calm breathing. It can feel good and is easy to fit in, but there is no good proof that it prevents delayed muscle soreness.

83.title: Mobility and Flexibility
83.short: Flexibility is the range a joint can move through, and mobility is your ability to control that range yourself. When you pick exercises, the range you can use with control counts for more than the deepest position you can reach.

84.title: Static and Dynamic Stretching
84.short: Static stretching holds a position, and dynamic stretching moves through a range under control. Both can help you prepare to move or improve flexibility when you match them to your goal and keep the intensity comfortable.

85.title: Hip Mobility
85.short: Hip mobility is comfortable movement at the hip joints: bending, extending, rotating and moving the leg to the side. It helps you reach useful squat, hinge and lunge positions, though hip anatomy and comfortable ranges differ from person to person.

86.title: Thoracic Spine and Shoulder Mobility
86.short: Your thoracic spine and shoulders take part in reaching, rotating, overhead pressing and many pulling movements. Mobility work can make these motions easier to reach, as long as you also build the strength and control to use them.

87.title: Recovery Between Sessions
87.short: Between sessions, fatigue fades and your body adapts to the training. A good plan mixes hard workouts with enough rest or lighter activity that you can keep performing week after week.

88.title: Sleep and Training
88.short: Sleep supports physical recovery, learning, mood and steady training performance. Adults generally need at least seven hours a night, and many do best with about seven to nine hours of good-quality sleep.

89.title: Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness
89.short: Delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS) is temporary tenderness and stiffness that often follows a new or unusually hard workout. It builds up after exercise and is often worst about 24–72 hours later.

90.title: Overreaching and Overtraining
90.short: Overreaching is a temporary drop in performance after you pile up more training stress than your body can recover from right now. True overtraining syndrome is more serious and lasts longer, and one bad workout can’t tell you that you have it.

91.title: Hydration
91.short: Staying hydrated supports circulation, temperature control and exercise performance. How much you need to drink depends on how much you sweat, the weather and how long you train, and drinking too much water can also be unsafe.

92.title: Nutrition Basics for Active People
92.short: Training goes better when you eat enough food, a variety of nutrients and enough protein for repair and adaptation. TrainUp teaches general nutrition principles and does not give meal plans, calorie targets or treatment diets.

93.title: Daily Readiness and Stress
93.short: Readiness is how prepared you feel and how well you perform going into a session. Poor sleep, illness and life stress can change how much training is right for you that day, even when the written plan stays the same.

94.title: Active Recovery
94.short: Active recovery is easy movement between harder training sessions. Walking, easy cycling and gentle mobility keep you moving without adding a second hard workout.

95.title: Technique Before Load
95.short: Good technique makes a movement repeatable and controlled before you add resistance. Increase the load only when you can keep your positions, your range of motion and your confidence.

96.title: Pain or Discomfort: How to Tell the Difference
96.short: Exercise often brings muscular effort, fatigue and short-lived soreness, but pain that is sharp, getting worse or comes with nerve symptoms needs attention. A simple symptom check helps you choose a safer next step without trying to diagnose anything.

97.title: Warning Signs: When to Stop Immediately
97.short: Some symptoms during exercise can signal an urgent medical problem instead of normal fatigue. Spotting them matters more than finishing the workout or hitting a planned target.

98.title: Axial Spinal Load
98.short: Axial spinal load is the compressive force that travels along your spine during movement or strength training. Knowing about it explains why some exercises may not suit you if you want options that load the spine less.

99.title: Training With Sensitive Knees
99.short: Sensitive knees can make some movements, depths or impact levels uncomfortable. Sensible training choices can cut down on avoidable flare-ups, but knee symptoms that persist or are severe need a professional assessment.

100.title: Training With a Sensitive Lower Back
100.short: A sensitive lower back can affect which loads, ranges and positions you tolerate during exercise. General fitness planning can favor comfortable variations and gradual progression, but it does not replace a clinical assessment or rehab.

101.title: Training With Sensitive Shoulders
101.short: How your shoulder feels can depend on the pressing angle, your grip, the range of motion and the load. Picking variations you tolerate helps you stay active, but shoulder pain with no clear cause, or pain that keeps going, needs a professional assessment.

102.title: Training With Sensitive Wrists
102.short: Your wrists may hurt when your hands carry your body weight or hold a load at an awkward angle. Changing the grip, the support or the exercise can sometimes ease the strain while you keep training the same movement pattern.

103.title: Coordination Difficulty and Safe Exercise Choice
103.short: Coordination difficulty is how much balance, timing and movement control an exercise asks of you. Matching it to your experience and how tired you are lets you practice good technique before you add speed or load.

104.title: Spotting and Safe Bailing
104.short: Spotting means someone helps you when you can’t finish a rep safely. Whether you train with a partner or alone, set up the rack properly, pick a weight you can control and know what you’ll do if a lift fails.

105.title: Starting From Zero
105.short: As a beginner, you can get fitter with a small routine you can repeat. In the first month, focus on learning the movements, keeping the effort comfortable and showing up regularly, and leave lifting the most weight possible for later.

106.title: Training After 50
106.short: You can still build strength and fitness after 50, and regular exercise helps you stay mobile and independent. Base your plan on your health, training history, balance and recovery. Being over 50 doesn’t mean you need the same easy routine as everyone else your age.

107.title: Strength Training for Teenagers
107.short: Supervised strength training designed for your age can help you build coordination, strength and confidence in how you move. Good technique and gradual progress come first, and copying an adult’s max-lifting program is the wrong model.

108.title: Exercise During Pregnancy and After Childbirth
108.short: Physical activity often helps during an uncomplicated pregnancy and after childbirth, but what your body needs can change a lot in these periods. Get individual advice from your obstetric care team, especially if you have symptoms or medical complications.

109.title: Starting Exercise With Excess Body Weight
109.short: People of every body size can get stronger, fitter and healthier with the right kind of activity. A good start focuses on comfort, lower impact and being able to do more, and body weight is only one of several ways to measure success.

110.title: Short Workouts for Busy Schedules
110.short: A well-planned 10–20 minute workout can build a training habit and improve your fitness. If you’re busy, short sessions you do often usually work better than an ambitious plan you can’t stick to.

111.title: Keeping a Training Log
111.short: A training log records what you planned, what you did and how it felt. Keeping it regularly helps you tell real progress from normal day-to-day ups and downs, and gives you better information when you change your program.

112.title: Measuring Strength Progress
112.short: Strength progress can show up as more reps, heavier loads or harder variations of an exercise. A fair comparison keeps your technique and conditions the same, and a personal record is only one of the numbers that count.

113.title: Measuring Conditioning Progress
113.short: Your conditioning is improving when you can keep going longer, cover a distance faster or do the same task with less effort. Repeating simple tests under similar conditions makes endurance trends easier to read.

114.title: Body Weight Trends and Measurements
114.short: Body weight and body measurements change for reasons besides gaining or losing fat, such as fluid and digestion. If you choose to track them, trends over time tell you more than single readings.

115.title: Simple Fitness Tests
115.short: Simple field tests give a quick snapshot of your strength endurance, balance or conditioning. They’re most useful when you repeat the same test the same way, and comparing yourself with one score meant for everyone tells you much less.

116.title: Adjusting the Plan From Feedback
116.short: Your plan works best when the work you completed and how it felt shape what comes next. Small, careful changes improve the fit. Change one thing at a time, and leave a workout as it is while you’re doing it.

117.title: Myth: You Can Burn Fat From One Body Part
117.short: Training your abs doesn’t let you reliably choose where your body loses fat. Targeted exercises strengthen the muscles you train, while where fat sits and how it changes depend on wider biological and behavioral factors.

118.title: Myth: Strength Training Makes Women Bulky
118.short: Resistance training doesn’t automatically make women look very muscular. The usual results are more strength and better muscle function, and how much visible muscle you gain depends on training, time, nutrition and your own biology.

119.title: Myth: Cardio Destroys Muscle Gains
119.short: Aerobic exercise and resistance training can work together in one fitness program. Some combinations may slightly reduce certain strength or power gains, but cardio doesn’t automatically cancel muscle growth.

120.title: Myth: No Pain, No Gain
120.short: Effort and gradually harder training build fitness, but you don’t need pain or severe soreness to improve. Aim for a challenge you can control, good technique and recovery, and don’t measure success by how much you suffer.
